skill.name: swarm
skill.description: Autonomous multi-agent workflow system for complex coding tasks. Use when the user requests non-trivial changes that would benefit from autonomous execution with built-in review gates. Ideal for refactoring modules, adding major features, migrating codebases, adding comprehensive test coverage, or any multi-step development task that can run autonomously. NOT for simple fixes, typos, or single-file changes.
skill.summary: Coordinate iterative coding agents with shared plans, review gates, tests, and completion checks.
skill.author: nbashaw

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown backticks, shell arithmetic, test commands, and local completion markers. One temporary-file issue is confirmed, and semantic review found a high-risk autonomous execution path that runs agents with reduced or disabled permission controls.

remediation.issue: Autonomous agents run through full-auto or permission-bypass modes.
remediation.suggestion: Use sandboxed agent modes, require confirmation for sensitive commands, and restrict execution to an isolated worktree or container.

remediation.issue: The test script creates a predictable file under /tmp.
remediation.suggestion: Create a private temporary directory with mktemp -d, store the plan inside it, and remove the directory through the existing trap.

semantic_findings.title: Autonomous Agents Run With Reduced Permission Controls
semantic_findings.description: The runner repeatedly launches Codex in full-auto mode or Claude with --dangerously-skip-permissions. Agents can edit files and run repository commands without per-action confirmation, increasing the impact of malicious repository content or flawed plans.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The executable script directly contains both reduced-confirmation command lines inside its autonomous iteration loop. The behavior is also described as intentional in the skill documentation.

content.value_statement: Complex coding work can lose context across many implementation and review steps. Swarm coordinates iterative agents through a shared plan, review gates, tests, and completion checks.
actual_capabilities: Interviews users to define goals, scope, plan location, and verification commands.
Creates Markdown plans with phases, checkboxes, role changes, and a shared progress log.
Runs sequential Codex or Claude agent iterations through a Bash script.
Adds reviewer, simplifier, tester, and gatekeeper stages to the execution plan.
Supports dry-run, verbose, agent selection, and configurable iteration limits.
Uses a project-local completion marker to stop the workflow.
limitations: Agents run sequentially rather than concurrently.
The runner requires Bash and an installed Codex or Claude command-line client.
Autonomous modes reduce permission prompts and should run only in an isolated worktree or container.
Plan quality and repository instructions directly affect execution quality and safety.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a coding task
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Swarm to plan [task]. Ask me for the goal, affected files, test commands, and preferred plan location before creating the plan.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a defined multi-file task

prompt_templates.title: Execute an approved plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Swarm to execute [plan file]. Start with a dry run, summarize the command, and wait for my approval before launching agents.

prompt_templates.title: Coordinate a migration
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Swarm plan for migrating [system] from [current state] to [target state]. Include rollback points, compatibility tests, and review gates.

prompt_templates.title: Run a constrained autonomous workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan and execute [goal] within [directories]. Use [test commands], preserve [constraints], stop on unexpected changes, and provide gatekeeper evidence before completion.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced workflow with strict scope and verification

output_examples.input: Plan a multi-file authentication refactor with unit and integration tests.
output: A phased plan covering discovery, implementation, migration, tests, and final review.
Named reviewer, simplifier, tester, and gatekeeper checkpoints.
A shared log format and measurable completion criteria.

output_examples.input: Run the approved migration plan in dry-run mode.
output_examples.output: A preview identifies the selected agent, plan path, iteration limit, completion marker, and command that would launch the workflow.
The completion report states the iteration count, gatekeeper decision, test status, change summary, and plan log location.

best_practices: Use measurable completion criteria and exact verification commands.
Review the generated plan and dry-run output before starting autonomous execution.
Run the workflow in an isolated worktree or container with limited credentials.
anti_patterns: Do not use Swarm for typos, single-line fixes, or tasks requiring frequent decisions.
Do not launch agents against an unreviewed plan or untrusted repository instructions.
Do not treat completion markers as proof without checking tests and gatekeeper evidence.

faq.question: Which tools does Swarm support?
faq.answer: It supports Codex, Claude, and Claude Code workflows through the included Bash runner and instructions.

faq.question: Does Swarm run agents in parallel?
faq.answer: No. The runner starts one agent iteration at a time and shares progress through the plan file.

faq.question: How does the workflow know when to stop?
faq.answer: A gatekeeper agent creates a project-local completion marker after checks pass. The runner also stops at the configured iteration limit.

faq.question: Can I preview execution first?
faq.answer: Yes. Dry-run mode prints the planned agent command without launching an agent.

faq.question: What permissions does the runner use?
faq.answer: Codex uses full-auto mode, while Claude uses a permission-bypass flag. Use an isolated environment and review the plan before execution.

faq.question: What tasks fit this skill?
faq.answer: Use it for multi-file features, refactors, migrations, or test expansions with clear goals and verification commands.
